entities.name: Vaux-le-Vicomte
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Vaux-le-Vicomte, a magnificent château located in the Île-de-France region of France, was commissioned by Nicolas Fouquet, the Superintendent of Finances, in 1656. This architectural masterpiece, designed by the architect Louis Le Vau, landscaped by André Le Nôtre, and adorned by painter Charles Le Brun, is emblematic of the French Baroque style, serving as a precursor to the grandeur of the Palace of Versailles. The château's opulent design and the political scandal surrounding its construction not only reflect the artistic trends of the period but also the intricate power dynamics of the French court under Louis XIV.

The construction of Vaux-le-Vicomte was marked by an extravagant expenditure that totaled approximately 20 million livres, a sum that raised eyebrows among the nobility and ultimately led to Fouquet's downfall. On August 17, 1661, a lavish fête held at the château was attended by King Louis XIV, who, feeling overshadowed by Fouquet’s display of wealth and artistry, promptly imprisoned him and seized the estate. This event catalyzed the king's subsequent efforts to assert his dominance through the construction of Versailles, wherein many elements of Vaux-le-Vicomte were emulated, demonstrating the château's profound influence on royal architecture.

The legacy of Vaux-le-Vicomte extends beyond its architectural significance; it became a symbol of the excesses of the ancien régime and the dangers of ambition at court. After Fouquet's imprisonment, the estate fell into disrepair until it was restored in the mid-20th century, becoming a site of cultural heritage and attracting visitors from around the globe. The château’s design principles influenced numerous other buildings in France and Europe, and its gardens set standards for landscape design that endure to this day.
